g.text: NEC infrared - the frame grammar, the repeat code, and what this act sends
the protocol's frame is 32 bits; this act sends the envelope around ONE byte
this gap is what tells a
TELL THE FRAME ENDED from a
A 0 and a 1 have the SAME burst and different gaps.
The burst is IDENTICAL, so the value is carried entirely by the silence. There
is no level to read and no clock to resynchronise to, which is why this is the
sharpest timing claim in the family: a gap 3 % long is still a zero, and a gap
Both bit values appear in the byte, and there are six transitions in eight. Its
bit-reverse is 0xA5 - it is a palindrome - and its complement is 0x5A, and
NEITHER is anything a wrong bit order produces by accident. So a firmware that
reversed the byte, complemented it, or rotated it cannot pass.
THE PROTOCOL'S REAL 32-BIT FRAME - NOT EXERCISED BY THIS ACT
in four bytes, each byte followed by its
one's complement, so a receiver can reject a frame corrupted on the way through
the air. The four are the ADDRESS of the remote and the COMMAND of the key, and
the inverses are the only error detection NEC has - there is no checksum, no
firmware/nec_ir.pe sends ONE byte, not four.
(leader, gap, eight slots, stop burst) is a correct NEC frame, and the payload
in it is 0xA5. So what this act proves is the FRAMING and the CARRIER; the
32-bit payload with its inverse bytes is not exercised, and the figure marks
those four boxes as unsent rather than drawing a frame the firmware does not
THE REPEAT CODE - NOT EXERCISED BY THIS ACT
different 16-bit sequence, not a repeat of the
32. While a key is held the remote re-sends a leader, a gap, and then
makes it unambiguous, because 0x00 is also a legitimate command code. A
receiver tells "held" from "pressed" by the 0x00/0xFF pair and by the ~40 ms
spacing, not by the byte count.
This act does not send it. The figure shows it because "how does a repeat code
differ from a frame" is the question the NEC frame diagram has to answer, and
answering it with only the frame would leave the question open.
same, 32 slots in a real frame
Frame length, and why a period error cannot make the frame
internally inconsistent. One byte is 32.06 ms: 9 + 4.5 + 8 x 2.25 + 0.5625.
The burst and the gap are independent counts, so an error in the carrier shows
up as a wrong frequency and an error in a gap shows up as a wrong slot - and
neither can quietly cancel the other inside one frame.
Green means measured in this simulation. Grey means the protocol has it and
this act does not send it. The distinction is drawn here rather than left
to the reader, because a diagram that draws the protocol's frame and does not
say which parts the firmware produces is a diagram that overstates the claim.
